before_manifest_row.title: The heat flow need not converge in supremum norm
before_manifest_row.statement: Let $n=1$ and let $f=\mathbf 1_{[0,\infty)}$, so that $f\in L^\infty(\mathbb R)\cap\bigcap_{1\le p<\infty}L^p(\mathbb R)$ and $f(0)=1$. Then for every $t>0$ $$H_tf(0)=\int_0^\infty\Gamma(y,t)\,dy=\frac12,\qquad\text{so}\qquad \sup_{x\in\mathbb R}|H_tf(x)-f(x)|\ge\frac12.$$ Hence the $p=\infty$ endpoint cannot be added to the $L^p$ convergence theorem: the distance at the jump does not decay, while convergence in $L^p$ for $1\le p<\infty$ still holds. Locally uniform convergence also fails on compact sets containing the jump, so the continuity hypothesis of the bounded-data theorem is not redundant, and its sharpening to a supremum-norm statement needs uniform continuity.
before_manifest_row.strategy: By symmetry of the Gaussian, $\int_0^\infty\Gamma(y,t)\,dy=\frac12$ for every $t>0$, so the value at the jump point stays at distance $\frac12$ from $f(0)=1$ for all times and the supremum does not tend to zero. Convergence in $L^p$ for finite $p$ is [[thm-heat-cauchy-solution-for-lp-data]]; locally uniform convergence away from the jump and the role of continuity are [[thm-heat-cauchy-solution-for-bounded-continuous-data]] and the published approximate-identity corollary. The construction is choice-free apart from the cited $L^p$ theorem.

current_statement:
Assuming Countable Choice, the claim that the $p=\infty$ endpoint can be added to the $L^p$ convergence
theorem for the heat flow, that is: for every
$f\in L^\infty(\mathbb R)\cap\bigcap_{1\le p<\infty}L^p(\mathbb R)$ one has
$\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}|H_tf(x)-f(x)|\to0$ as $t\downarrow0^+$. This fails even
for the simplest jump data, and locally uniform convergence on compact sets
containing the jump fails as well. The same witnesses also obstruct convergence
in the essential supremum norm: for $f=\mathbf1_{[0,\infty)}$ one has
$H_tf(0)=1/2$ and $\|H_tf-f\|_\infty\ge1/2$; for
$f_0=\mathbf1_{[0,1)}$, which belongs to every finite $L^p$ and to $L^\infty$,
one has $H_tf_0(0)<1/2$ and $\|H_tf_0-f_0\|_\infty>1/2$ for every $t>0$. Thus the continuity hypothesis cannot be discarded;
actual supremum convergence for bounded real data requires uniform continuity,
and essential supremum convergence requires a uniformly continuous representative.
